localChanges: The map used to build its scenery on six separate world-sized canvases and stack them up on every redraw, then composite every one of them at every wrapped position — including positions entirely off the screen. It draws the same picture from one canvas now, and only over the part of the screen it actually covers: sixty draws and nearly three hundred megapixels a frame down to fifteen and seven and a half, and about ninety megabytes of memory handed back (#7).

The minimap turned out to be the more expensive half, once the map stopped drowning it out. It made its picture by shrinking three full-size copies of the world down to a couple of hundred pixels across, every time anything changed. It has a small picture of its own now, drawn at the size it is actually shown: terrain in flat colours, cities in their owner's colour so you can see whose land is whose, and nothing at all where you have not been yet (#53).

The unit waiting for orders shows there as a flashing white tile, so you can find it at a glance and click straight to it. Clicking takes you where you clicked, too — it used to land two tiles up and to the left (#54).

The minimap is drawn at a whole number of pixels per tile and scaled up, rather than squeezed down to a fractional size, so it is sharp for the first time. And the box showing the part of the world you are looking at comes back round the other side when the map wraps, instead of running off the edge and leaving half of itself behind.
